events.title: Asia’s safe harbour for wealth
events.summary: OCBC’s long-standing presence in the region gives it a perspective shaped by decades of experience in key financial centres [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Global markets have rarely lacked opportunity, but the conditions affecting them have become far more difficult to read. Geopolitical tensions and rapid technological change can reshape both investment and business outlooks. For high-net-worth (HNW) individuals, returns obviously remain important, but they are increasingly considered alongside institutional strength, regulatory stability and the ability to keep long-term plans on course. Founded in Singapore in 1932, OCBC has built a strong presence across Asia over more than 90 years. Today, as one of Singapore’s leading financial institutions and the second-largest financial services group in Southeast Asia by assets, OCBC brings together deep regional insights, strong governance and a long-standing commitment to serving clients across generations. This blend of regional experience and institutional resilience enables OCBC to support clients as they navigate opportunities and challenges with confidence across a diverse range of markets. Singapore’s stable and well-regulated financial environment provides an important foundation for individuals and businesses with needs across the region. Underpinned by transparent institutions, strong rule of law and political stability, it offers a degree of clarity that can be particularly valuable when making long-term decisions. Complementing this environment is OCBC’s deep Asian heritage and extensive regional network, which provide valuable perspectives shaped by decades of operating across diverse markets and economic cycles. For HNW individuals, this heritage, combined with Singapore’s governance standards, addresses two different but equally important needs. The first brings familiarity with the commercial and investment landscape across the Asean bloc and greater China, while the second provides a disciplined, structured environment in which financial and business interests can be managed. Combining the two enables clients to assess opportunities in Asia through Singapore’s robust governance framework and OCBC’s deep understanding of regional markets. These qualities continue to resonate with individuals, families and businesses seeking continuity, trusted partnerships and institutional strength. For those whose priorities span multiple markets, a relationship built on deep regional experience can provide greater confidence as circumstances evolve over time. Staying connected across markets and generations OCBC Premier Banking draws on the bank’s established presence across Asia, including Singapore and Hong Kong, to provide greater continuity and support for clients whose needs extend across multiple markets. That footprint can make it more straightforward to manage financial arrangements across markets without treating each as a separate relationship. Clients can benefit from insights shaped by OCBC’s experience across the wider region. Over time, priorities naturally evolve across life stages and generations. Having a trusted banking partner that understands these changing needs can provide continuity and support throughout that journey. In this context, the value of OCBC Premier Banking lies in the relationship it builds with clients. Digital tools such as the OCBC app can support everyday needs, while a digital wallet is also available, which can be used for banking and payments in 19 currencies. In addition, there are dedicated relationship managers and wealth specialists who provide personalised advice to support the needs of clients. Beyond banking and financial services, clients can access a tailored concierge service covering lifestyle experiences, wellness, children’s education, and relocation support, providing personalised assistance and greater convenience. In addition, OCBC Premier Banking clients have access to more than 60 Premier Centres across Asia, with free cash withdrawal services at OCBC ATMs in Malaysia, Hong Kong, Macau and Indonesia. OCBC Bank is part of the OCBC One Group, an ecosystem that includes the Bank of Singapore, Great Eastern for insurance services, Lion Global Investors for asset management and OCBC Securities – the bank’s brokerage firm for stockbroking services. This network allows clients to gain access to a comprehensive range of financial services. As clients’ priorities evolve over time, OCBC continues to support them with the strength of its regional network, institutional expertise and long-standing commitment to building trusted relationships. In a world of shifting tides, OCBC remains Asia’s trusted harbour for wealth – bringing together stability, connectivity and more than 90 years of experience serving clients across the region.

Madonna took home three trophies, including Artist of the Year, while Taylor Swift left with two, though one of them was the night's biggest prize. Madonna led the nominations for the first time in 28 years, her 13 nods pipping Swift's 11. Sabrina Carpenter joined Madonna to open the show with a version of Bring Your Love, their duet from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II, which later won the Best Collaboration award on the night. Charli XCX then emerged to perform their track Danceteria Afterhours. This opener won't grab the headlines like 2003's infamous kiss, but reminded fans and naysayers of Madge's continued skills as a performer. Madonna beat just about everyone — Taylor, Sabrina, Ariana — to win the Artist of the Year award and backed that up with Best Dance to bring her haul for the night to three. "Most of you were probably not born, but I performed at the first MTV awards 43 years ago," Madonna said in her speech accepting Artist of the Year. As with any awards show, the night began with a focus on arrivals. Here's what some of the stars wore on the red carpet. While Madonna took home more trophies, Swift did get the big one, winning Video of the Year for The Fate of Ophelia. Swift was also a record-breaker before this year's ceremony even started. Tied with Beyoncé at 30 wins apiece before the 2026 VMAs, she took the lead by winning the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, announced before the ceremony began. As a director, Swift has won four VMAs — more than anyone in history. She used the moment to premiere the video for her song Patient Zero, featuring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell. Swift left with two awards from her 11 nominations. Snoop Dogg promises weed to winners As the host of the awards show, Snoop Dogg arrived on stage to rapturous applause and his song Who Am I (What's My Name)? from his 1993 album Doggystyle. It was a sign of things to come, with Snoop classics playing in the background whenever he hit the stage. "Welcome to the 2026 MTV VMAs," he said. "I'm your host with the most, the D-O-double-G Big Snoop Dogg." Snoop Dogg hosted the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards held in Los Angeles, California. ( Getty Images: Rich Polk/Billboard ) Snoop told the audience that Madonna killed it with her performance, which opened the show. "One thing I want to say is, she ain't a virgin no more." Snoop went on to say that when he was first asked to host the awards show, he asked if it would be in Los Angeles. When the answer was no, that was his answer too, with the rapper telling organisers he was busy. "Then they called me back and said, 'Hold on, Mr Dogg, it's in LA now.'" Unless you've been living under a rock, you'll be well aware that Snoop Dogg is more than just a little bit partial to taking a puff or two of marijuana. He went on to promise the biggest party the VMAs had ever seen, and some special "sticky-icky-icky" to the winners. "But everybody else, look under your seat," he said, before quipping: "There should be nothing there." Snoop gave a roll call of some of his "favourite people" who he said he was grateful to be in the company of at the ceremony. "Madonna, Taylor Swift. Shaboozey, Lisa, Bruno Mars and my girl Raye, just to name a few," he said. "Now, we got a lot of people in here tonight that's ready to party." He also said the show would honour some of the most iconic bands and artists of all time including Nirvana, George Michael and Dolly Parton. For his day one fans, Snoop harkened back to his Deeez Nuuuts skit on Dr Dre's The Chronic. He then introduced Teyana Taylor to introduce the first award of the night. Nirvana, Dolly Parton, George Michael honoured If you need proof the VMAs is all about pop: this year they discontinued the Best Rock Video award. Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear of Nirvana accept the Video Vanguard Award. ( Getty Images: Rich Polk/Billboard ) But the impact of grunge icons Nirvana defies genre, their Vanguard Award further evidence of their enduring influence. "Their sound was loud, beautiful, daringly open," Public Enemy's Chuck D said when presenting the award. "Their lyrics were poetic, raw and deeply human. "Their music videos defined an era.

events.title: Dubai’s Sobha Realty seeks $600m US housing push and targets further expansion
events.summary: Dubai developer Sobha Realty is investing $600 million to build about 700 homes in Texas as it expands in the US, with plans to enter more cities across the world’s largest economy, a senior executive has said. The company, which began US operations last year, has acquired about 105 hectares across Celina and Frisco in the fast-growing Dallas-Fort Worth metropolitan area, where it plans to develop single-family homes over five phases in the next five years. Sales of the first 34 homes in Celina are expected to begin next year, with prices from $1 million to $1.5 million, Vipin Das, chief executive of Sobha Realty US, told The National . The projects will be funded through a mix of debt and its own equity, with the company raising local debt. “Last week we got the first development loan approved for our first two projects from Bank7 and CCB, so that's good news for us,” Mr Das said. Demand for homes It owns 64 hectares of land in Celina and another 40 in Frisco, with demand for housing mainly coming from residents and corporate employees. “In Frisco there is a lot of Asian community living and in Celina it’s a kind of healthy mix, with people wanting more space as they upgrade their life and move into a bigger space … a move-up home or second move-up home for a bigger family,” he said. Demand is also coming from new corporate offices, including a Goldman Sachs campus that will accommodate 5,000 employees and regional headquarters for the New York Stock Exchange in Dallas. Telecom giant AT&T is moving its base from Downtown Dallas to Plano, which is creating new demand for housing in North Dallas. “The trend we are seeing towards the north is growing. We are very well positioned within the corridor of growth, where Frisco, Plano and … further growth to Celina is happening.” Demand for housing remained resilient in Texas, with June closed sales volumes rising 8.6 per cent on an annual basis to 34,956, according to the Texas Real Estate Research Centre. The average sales price for homes hit $342,900 in June. The company plans to expand into other cities in the US to create a “national presence”, Mr Das added. Houston, Austin, Nashville, Phoenix and Florida are being targeted as places in which to build. “We are seriously exploring Houston. We are very seriously exploring Austin.” Sobha is also looking to expand in Australia after acquiring land in Brisbane and the Gold Coast, Mr Das said. Construction is expected to begin there next year following the approval process, he added, without divulging the full details. Sobha was founded by PNC Menon, who began his entrepreneurial journey with an interior decorating company in Oman in the 1970s. The firm has been rapidly expanding in the UAE, with projects in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Umm Al Quwain. It launched a Dh40 billion ($10.9 billion) residential project in Abu Dhabi, marking its entry into the emirate's residential sector this year. Sobha reported total sales of Dh30 billion last year, up 30 per cent annually, with growth driven by its projects in Dubai and Umm Al Quwain. It also unveiled a Dh50 billion development in Dubai in January as it continues to grow its property portfolio in the emirate.

events.title: Amazon evaluating drone deliveries in Australia, Asia
events.summary: E-commerce giant Amazon.com is preparing to launch drone deliveries in Australia and other nations. “As Prime Air evaluates Australia and other countries, we are hiring a Head of Regulatory Approvals, Australia – the person responsible for navigating Australia's aviation regulatory system and securing every approval required to deliver to Australian customers by drone,” reads a recently published job ad. Whoever gets the gig in Australia will report to someone who holds the title “Leader, Prime Air Expansion – Asia Pacific.” The Register asked Amazon to comment on the ad, and which other Asian countries it plans to enter. The company had not responded at the time of writing. The successful applicant “will be measured by the approvals you obtain, the timelines you hit, and – ultimately – Australian customers receiving drone deliveries.” That wording suggests Amazon intends to operate Prime Air in Australia and is doing rather more than market evaluations. In August, Amazon said it plans to operate Prime Air drones in “nearly” 500 cities and towns across the USA this year. Meta and Singapore sling scammers Meta last week announced that information-sharing with Singapore Police helped the social media giant to identify a new variety of attack and led it to take action against more than 113,000 entities and pages connected to fraud and scams on Facebook and Instagram. Meta calls the new scams calls “shell pages” and says they “look empty and harmless” because they don’t include ads or content that violates Zuck’s T&Cs. “But scammers had pre-built infrastructure, ready to be activated for scam campaigns at a moment’s notice,” Meta says. “Working from SPF’s signals, in July 2026, we took action against over 3.6 million shell pages before they could be used – and we’re now pursuing further disruptions against this type of scam.” “Rather than responding to individual reports, this collaboration focuses on proactive network disruption – where SPF information helps Meta’s investigators identify and dismantle entire ecosystems of bad actors,” the company asserted. Meta didn’t say how scammers could sign up for 3.6 million pages without it noticing. Nothing has a plan to conquer India’s consumer tech market Consumer electronics outfit Nothing, which has carved out a small niche with well-priced Android devices, has decided to spin out its Indian subsidiary CMF. CEO Carl Pei explained the move as a bet on India’s growing electronics manufacturing industry spurring demand for local consumer tech brands. “Every country that has manufactured consumer electronics at scale has eventually produced its own global champions. Japan did. Korea did. China did, and I watched it happen over the better part of a decade living there,” he wrote. “India is next. It's already the world's second largest smartphone manufacturer, with the largest youth population on earth and one of its deepest software talent pools. What it doesn't have yet is a global consumer electronics brand of its own. That will change. The only questions are when, and how.” Pei thinks the how is spinning out CMF, a Nothing sub-brand that makes budget-priced phones, audio kit, and smartwatches. Bangkok floods – brace for supply chain impact When heavy rains and subsequent floods struck Thailand’s capital city Bangkok in 2011, facilities operated by hard disk manufacturers Western Digital and Seagate experienced damage that disrupted production for months. Bangkok was again hit by rain and severe floods last weekend, but to date The Register can find no evidence of problems at major tech companies. Western Digital and Seagate have not announced any issues, while hyperscalers Google, Microsoft, and AWS also report their local infrastructure is operating normally. Thailand’s government announced a two-day holiday to help residents clean up after the flood, which saw much of Bangkok under 30 centimeters or more of water. events.title: AOC test-runs a Senate bid in upstate New York
events.summary: BUFFALO, N.Y. — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's flirtation with a 2028 Senate bid is getting real — more real than the presidential buzz around her might suggest. She's barnstorming through upstate New York, meeting with local officials, and kicking off a voter turnout program that could help her collect valuable data for a possible Senate campaign. Why it matters: Whether the House member from New York runs for Senate or the White House is one of the biggest questions hanging over the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. Zoom in: Her swing through Buffalo and Ithaca was officially aimed at boosting Democratic turnout in the midterms. But it doubled as a way to test AOC's appeal far from her home base of Queens and the Bronx, and build relationships with locals. In Buffalo, she met privately with Mayor Sean Ryan, then held an impromptu press conference with him, generating coverage of the duo on local TV news. She and her team later kicked off a voter-turnout operation that could help them gather information about the electorate outside New York City. "I want to be very forthright about our intentions here, which is to transform the state of New York," Ocasio-Cortez told activists in a Buffalo arts center who were attending a training session of hers aimed at getting inactive voters to the polls. In Ithaca, she appeared at an apple festival with Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.) and on Sunday was scheduled to headline a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall. It's friendly terrain: The city is home to several democratic socialist elected officials, and Ocasio-Cortez is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. The intrigue: AOC says she's genuinely undecided on whether to run for the White House or Senate. Her recent activities upstate suggested that wasn't a head fake. Ryan said Ocasio-Cortez has been talking with state officials about how help communities beyond New York City. Meanwhile, some influential Democrats in early presidential primary states have told us they haven't yet heard from AOC. And she hasn't made public visits this year to some of those early states, a contrast from other potential 2028 contenders who are practically living in them. Many political insiders believe that if Ocasio-Cortez were to run for an open Senate seat, she'd clear the Democratic field. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who's in his fifth term, hasn't said whether he'll run for reelection. AOC was greeted like a rock star on her upstate tour, with Ryan remarking that at City Hall "a young man really, literally shouted across the lobby, like, 'Oh my gosh, congresswoman, can I take a picture with you?'" Yes, but: Ocasio-Cortez also has taken several steps that could point toward a presidential run. She's toured the country, moderated her stance on some cultural issues, and opened up about her egg-freezing journey. She recently told the New York Times she'll consider whether to run for president after the midterms. Between the lines: One exchange with Ocasio-Cortez offered a window into how she is approaching her decision. We asked her how she's thinking about the future of the progressive movement as she weighs a White House run. In the last two open Democratic presidential primaries, there has been a clear progressive standard-bearer, and many on the left think she's their only hope for 2028. She didn't seem persuaded that by that argument. "The movement is so much bigger than any one person," she told us. The bottom line: AOC suggested that her choice won't be solely about ideology. "These decisions aren't always about punditry or ideology. It's about putting the country first," she said. "What's important is ending … the corrupt reign of the Trump administration, as well as any of its acolytes." Asked whether that means she's weighing "electability" as she determines her next move, she replied, "I don't see who wouldn't."

( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) Homes affected by the River Murray flood event in 2022 are still waiting for repairs. Nationally, there is a 141,000-person skilled workers shortage, according to Master Builders Australia. The SA and federal governments have committed funding to help cover the travel expenses of rural or regional apprentices travelling long distances to keep them on the job. For almost four years, Jamie Bruce has been sleeping on a fold-out couch. Their family home at Morgan was inundated by floodwater during South Australia's third-largest River Murray flood in 2022, just 10 months after moving in. Before: The Bruce family home in 2022. . . After: The Bruce family home in 2026. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition It destroyed the lower level of the home, washing away Jamie's bedroom and identity. "I was just starting to decorate the walls and get things to a state where the space was me," they said. Jamie Bruce is still sleeping on a fold-out couch waiting for the house repairs to be finished. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "Then I watched my little dragons that were on the wall slowly disappear under the water." Floodwaters peaked at 186 gigalitres a day, leaving only concrete and wooden cladding behind in Jamie's bedroom. The family's staircase is being held up by two wooden panels. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) Jamie's mum, Kay Bruce, describes the first 12 months following the flood as "a nightmare". The family spent five of those months living out of a friend's large tin shed. "Thinking about [that time] now still brings tears to my eyes," Ms Bruce said. Frustrated by the delay for their insurer to send out a tradie, the family took a payout so they could source their own workers. "[I had] so many phone calls where they would never come back to me," she said. Kay Bruce says the situation has taken a mental and physical toll on her family. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "I've got a spreadsheet, and it shows just name after name after name." Despite trying to project-manage the rebuild, after three years Ms Bruce was still yet to have a tradesperson follow through and do the job. "I can't understand when people make arrangements to come and do work or make quotes and then just don't turn up, don't phone you, don't text you," she said. Her husband, Rob Bruce, said that while the process had been exhausting for the whole family, it came with a level of guilt. "We have friends that lost their entire place and they're still in the caravan park whilst their houses are being built," Mr Bruce said. "We'd feel bad knowing that our place was all done and they're still in the caravan park waiting." With the cost of materials to build a home spiking in recent years, Mr Bruce said the family felt trepidation about the future. "It worries me that it's going to be a hit for us [to rebuild]," he said. The cost to build a new home in South Australia has risen by almost 40 per cent since 2021, according to the Insurance Council of Australia. It is something social policy, climate and international engagement manager Alix Pearce says is a growing national issue. "We're seeing this [rise] in materials and labour costs, too; for example, roof tiles have gone up 77 per cent over the last five years." Alix Pearce says governments need to increase investment in resilience to build stronger homes. ( ABC News: Greg Bigelow ) Ms Pearce said state and federal governments needed to do more to uplift their investment in housing resilience and address tradie shortages across the country. "We need to see increased investment in trades and construction, particularly in those high-risk areas in Australia." There is currently a 141,000-person skilled workers shortage nationally, according to Master Builders Australia. In South Australia, about 20,000 workers are required over the next five years to meet major project and housing demand, according to a state government spokesperson. The spokesperson said it has committed $11 million over the next two years, alongside the federal government, to help the travel expenses of rural or regional apprentices travelling long distances to keep them on the job. Master Builders Australia projects a worker shortage of 935,600 by 2035. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "The new measure will support an additional 400 regional apprentices and trainees to undertake their training," the statement said.

events.title: Walmart denies using personal info to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels
events.summary: Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology. NEW YORK -- Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores. In a statement posted on the company's website, Walmart Inc.'s CEO John Furner vowed that the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer isn't using personal information like income, shopping history or a customer's willingness to pay to set prices, and it won't be doing so in the future either. “We don’t set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” Furner wrote Friday. “Whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.” The pledge from Walmart comes as concerns are mounting from some shoppers, consumer advocates and lawmakers skeptical about the rollout of digital price labels by the discounter and other stores. Digital price labels are rapidly replacing paper shelf tags at U.S. supermarkets and let stores change prices instantly from a central computer instead of having workers swap out paper labels by hand. Furner noted that Walmart is also holding its artificial intelligence shopping assistant Sparky to the same promise and won't be using the bot to raise a customer's price or hide lower-priced options that meet their needs. Furner said such practices would violate the company's “every day low prices” business model. He also noted that prices can change: Walmart lowers them when it can pass savings along, or sometimes raises them because an item costs more to buy or to transport, he said. District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' UK police arrest 5 men under terrorism, explosives acts close to US air base White House orders over $800M in funds rescinded Walmart said in March that 2,300 Walmart U.S. locations already use digital shelves, and it expects this technology to be chain-wide within the next year. Walmart executives have repeatedly said it uses electronic shelf price tags to help the retailer change prices consistently and match what rings up at checkout. It also saves workers time and reduces labor costs by replacing paper tags. Last month, the Federal Trade Commission said that it's putting companies on notice that the practice of personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws. The agency said it does not have the legal authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances, but it issued a new bulletin that warned companies that they must disclose to customers how the personal information is being used to set a price. events.title: SA's statewide blackout was 10 years ago — but electricity debate is still live
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis inspected damaged towers near Melrose in the aftermath of the blackout. ( ABC News: Dean Faulkner ) Blackouts come in different forms — there are those that affect memory, and those that affect electricity. But no mental blank has impaired the vividness of Tom Koutsantonis's recollection of the time when, on a tempestuous spring afternoon 10 years ago, power was cut to the whole of South Australia. Reflecting on the precise moment when the statewide blackout began, the Labor MP smiled wryly at the irony of the circumstances in which he found himself at the time. "I was actually in the parliament on my feet moving legislation relating to the National Electricity Market (NEM)," he said recently. About 4pm on September 28, 2016, electricity supply to more than 850,000 properties and approximately 1.7 million residents was disrupted, leaving South Australia in darkness. Police directing traffic around Adelaide's CBD during the blackout a decade ago. ( AAP: David Mariuz ) Mr Koutsantonis was then the state's minister for energy — a portfolio which, despite changes of government in the intervening years, he holds again today. His first inkling that something was wrong was prompted by an apparent malfunction at the entrance to the parliamentary chamber. The billionaire bet that created the first big battery For former SA premier Jay Weatherill, the tweets that triggered the Tesla giant battery project created an opportunity — but also a shock. Suspecting there had been "some sort of brownout", he was then told by an advisor that what had occurred was far worse than that. In the same moment that Mr Koutsantonis heard parliament's doors start to glitch, energy industry analyst Danny Price was on his computer monitoring the situation closely. "I just saw demand drop off a cliff, so I knew straightaway it was a blackout," he said. "I wasn't surprised — I was watching the weather in South Australia for a day or two beforehand. You could see a very big storm was brewing." While supply was slowly restored over the coming hours, some parts of the state were without power for more than two days . A map from the time of the blackout showing outages across South Australia. ( SA Power Networks ) An early estimate of the economic impact concluded that the blackout cost businesses more than $360 million — but money wasn't everything . At Flinders Medical Centre, there were distressing consequences for prospective parents when dozens of embryos were lost at a private fertility clinic because mains supply was cut. At different times, energy policy, renewables and extreme weather have each been lambasted as the prime culprit for the statewide blackout. In a 2017 report, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) concluded that overly sensitive protection mechanisms in some of the state's wind farms were to blame . "Activation of this protection feature resulted in a significant sustained power reduction for these wind farms," the report stated. A lone policeman directs traffic near Victoria Square during the 2016 blackout. ( ABC News: Tony Hill ) AEMO found that the sudden dip in output triggered a power surge along the Heywood Interconnector from Victoria, which in turn caused the system to trip and SA to become "islanded" from the rest of the NEM. "AEMO cannot rule out the possibility that later events could have caused a black system, but is not aware of any system damage that would have done this." But the causes that were most immediately obvious on the day itself were the tornadoes, with estimated wind speeds of between 190 and 260 km/h, that ripped through SA's mid north , damaging critical infrastructure. A collapsed transmission tower near Melrose during a severe storm at the time. ( ABC News: Dean Faulkner ) Indeed, the most enduring imagery from the blackout is probably that of giant transmission towers lying collapsed and contorted in fields . "Two towers had been taken down by a freak tornado or hurricane," Mr Koutsantonis said. "Any time you take out transmission lines … you're going to have a shock to the system. "That caused a sudden loss of power and the system reacted according to the laws of physics." Energy economist Danny Price says renewables need the support of thermal generation. ( ABC News ) Mr Price also pointed to the weather — but said there was a failure of preparation at market level ahead of a "one-in-50-year storm". "[There were not] any gas generators running, which is crazy to me," he said.

events.title: Amodei critics target Trump with hit piece before White House dinner
events.summary: Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump , per an Axios review of the document. Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension. Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties." It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump." The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear. It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!" Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise. Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company . Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology. Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore. "The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios. The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first. Marc Caputo contributed to this story

( ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton ) After four decades as a Commonwealth Bank customer, Trevor Vienet is changing banks. That is because CBA has changed its association with the Qantas Frequent Flyer program ahead of the credit and debit surcharge ban announced by the Reserve Bank of Australia. It is the lesser-known side effect of the changes that begin on October 1 because banks' revenue will drop as they reduce the amount they charge businesses to bank with them. The Commonwealth Bank has introduced a new in-house rewards system called Yello, which Mr Vienet is not eligible for. "The [CBA] letter was, I'd call it a Dear John letter. It's like: 'You've had a long relationship, but it's all over,'" he said. After decades with the Commonwealth Bank, Trevor Viénet is moving much of his banking elsewhere. ( ABC News: Matthew Holmes ) From Thursday, businesses will be banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa. The cap on interchange fees paid by Australian businesses to banks for processing credit card fees will reduce from 0.8 per cent to 0.3 per cent, meaning businesses will pay lower fees but bank revenues will take a hit. In preparation for these changes, the major Australian banks are increasing credit card fees, reducing reward program perks and cutting back on travel insurance inclusions. "I was pretty angry … I've been a customer for 40 years, have held several accounts and three mortgages and paid those off," Mr Vienet said. The surcharge ban is expected to save consumers about $1.6 billion and businesses $200 million in surcharge fees annually. The changes to interchange fees — the fees banks charge businesses for using their systems — are estimated to reduce transaction fees from businesses to banks by about $910 million each year. Sally Tindall is the data insights director at Canstar. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Canstar's data insights director, Sally Tindall, said it was clear the banks were not willing to wear the reduction in interchange fees. "They're looking to recoup at least some of that loss … the consumer, in many cases, will end up paying for part of this ban at the minimum, but also small businesses." But Australian Banking Association (ABA) chief executive Simon Birmingham said the changes implemented by the banks were expected. "That was one of the things that the Reserve Bank called out as not only expecting to see, but basically wanting to see," he said. Do you know more, or are you affected? Tell us here . Small businesses say prices may rise The almost one in six businesses that surcharge have until October 1 to make the necessary changes, and some are worried. Swim school owner Greg Hodge is working with his customers to change the way they pay for lessons, from credit card payments to bank transactions. Greg Hodge says the ban on surcharges will force him to increase the cost of swimming lessons. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) But if they can not switch to bank transfers, Mr Hodge may have to charge extra for each lesson to cover all banking costs. He is not alone. Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief executive Wes Lambert said many businesses were considering their options. "Many have indicated that they are going to increase their prices," he said. "Many have [also] told us they are going to stop taking certain credit card types [and] many have said that they're going to go to cash only." Despite the additional charging that may happen, the RBA's head of payments policy, Ellis Connolly, said he did not expect increases would have an "ongoing effect on inflation". Ellis Connolly says the surcharging changes will not have an ongoing effect on inflation. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "In the end, the consumer was paying it either way, whether it was paid in a surcharge or whether it was paid in the end price," he said. While some businesses may be forced to increase the prices of goods and services, others have argued it is not that simple. Central Coast councillor Jared Wright said for a council to increase fees, it had to go through a "multi-month process" involving public consultation. He estimated the impact of the surcharge ban on his council, which is one of the largest in New South Wales, would be about $400,000 in lost fees, and was concerned about the possible flow-on effect to his constituents.

events.title: 'Something we've never seen before': The risk of AI bioweapons
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How concerning is the biological weapon threat from AI systems? AI tools raise the risk that someone could develop a biological weapon. ( Supplied: Geralt/Pixabay ) The AI industry is suddenly rife with existential fears, with senior figures claiming it could "kill us all" within a decade. Dario Amodei, CEO of one of the world's largest AI companies, Anthropic, has called for a "slowdown" of AI development to prevent it outrunning our control. One particular fear is that AI could develop a dangerous biological agent, or a bioweapon. At the same time, biologists are showing AI can help them with useful research — including those employed at Anthropic, who have just announced AI has helped them discover a new class of enzymes they claim "could represent a new gene editing mechanism ". So is AI a biological threat, or a boon? It may be an uneasy mixture of both. Why does AI raise the danger of bioweapons? Labs around the world have had the tools to make dangerous biological agents, like viruses, for decades. But few people have known how to use those tools, and all of them are scientists who have spent years building their qualifications and credibility. Brendan Walker-Munro, a security researcher at Southern Cross University, says AI changes this. David Heslop, a public health researcher at the University of New South Wales, says the speed of AI progress makes him "very concerned". "The tools are advancing at a rate which means that human oversight is becoming challenging," Dr Heslop says. AI is moving at a pace that makes it hard for traditional biosecurity to keep up. ( Unsplash: João Pessoa ) An advanced AI model could give a user outside traditional systems the information required to make a bioweapon. "It could be a virus or it could be a bacteria, it could be a fungus, it could be something we've never seen before." Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is calling on the industry to slow down. Equally dangerously, in Dr Heslop's opinion, an AI tool like a large language model (LLM) could help a bad actor plan to deploy dangerous material, including pre-existing viruses or toxins. Such work would still need a level of expertise and tens of thousands of dollars of lab equipment. "We're not at the point, yet, where the LLM gives you a superpower," Dr Heslop says. "But it's certainly something that could be done in a laboratory." AI could also be used to attack broader public health systems, like hospital infrastructure. David Kainer, a computational biologist at the University of Queensland, says the same tools applied to plant science could "potentially destroy large amounts of food production". "You could imagine something similar happening to engineer super-pathogens for crops." What sorts of biological threats has AI enabled? There are several cases where AI has already been used to help design dangerous biological agents. In 2022, researchers at the Collaborations Pharmaceuticals company showed they could use their company's AI software to make dangerous toxins . The company's AI tool was used to screen out drug candidates with high predicted toxicity. But the team found they could instruct it to do the opposite, designing new toxins in a matter of hours. Getting AI 'drunk' makes it more likely to break rules, research finds North Korean hackers steal millions in crypto heist OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT Reporting rogue AI won't be enough to keep Australia safe, expert warns In its recent threat intelligence report , Anthropic highlighted five examples of people using its products "in ways that could support biological weapons development". Anthropic's models were used to do things like draft grant applications and analyse data in research that made human viruses more contagious, and venoms and toxins more deadly. All of these users, according to Anthropic, were "working scientists" outside the US using unauthorised software to gain access to the US versions of their products. Anthropic banned the users for violating supported region policies. Are there legitimate reasons for using AI? Biologists have used AI for positive purposes. AI program Alphafold, for instance, has been used to predict the shape of proteins for medicinal research, winning its creators the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. More recently, US researchers used generative AI to design new bacteria-infecting viruses that could become treatments against infection.

events.title: What to know about maximising the range of your electric vehicle
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How to maximise your EV's range while spending as little as possible From one-pedal breaking to ditching your roof racks, there are ways to make your EV's charge last longer. ( Unsplash ) If you're among the many Australians who have bought an electric vehicle this year, maximising the range of your new ride might be on your mind. EVs have improved greatly in terms of range but still use more energy during longer freeway-type drives, and while charging an EV is significantly cheaper than refuelling with petrol or diesel , there's still money to be saved by using them more efficiently. Experts say getting the most out of an EV battery isn't that different to getting good value from a tank of fuel, but there are some key differences to be aware of. Regenerative braking and one-pedal driving The one big advantage EVs have is the ability to create their own power via regenerative braking. "When [an EV] goes into slowdown, then it's actually acting as a generator," says Australian Electric Vehicle Association technical convenor Michael Day, based in Epping, NSW, on Dharug country. Regenerative braking can be turned on and off, but he says newer EVs have it turned on by default. You can also take advantage of regenerative braking by practising one-pedal driving, which actually involves using the brake as little as possible. "You just ease on and ease off the accelerator pedal," says Electric Vehicle Council senior policy manager Bjorn Siem, who works in Meanjin/Brisbane. Bjorn Siem is the Electric Vehicle Council's senior policy manager. ( Supplied: Electric Vehicle Council ) "It's a little bit strange to begin with … but once you get used to it, it's brilliant." Mr Day uses one-pedal braking "all the time". "Not in an unsafe way … you tend to be able to moderate the momentum of the car better with the throttle and then use the brakes as an emergency stop when you really need to," he says. For new owners, some of the fun of EVs is their "get up and go", Mr Day says. Over the past year, electric car sales have tripled, as anxiety about fuel shortages and rising petrol prices continues. But as with combustion-engine cars, avoiding the temptation to make a fast getaway at every set of traffic lights can go a long way to using less battery power and preserving your EV's range. "Most electric vehicles … can get off the line quite quickly," Mr Day says. Make freeway driving more efficient Where you're driving can also affect your EV's range, says RACV motoring editor Terry Martin, who lives in South Gippsland on Gunaikurnai and Bunurong country. Slowing down and switching on your EV's cruise control or autopilot function can help preserve change on long trips. ( Unsplash ) "EVs are better suited to stop-start driving in the city, when the car can recover energy through regenerative braking and so forth," he says. However, the experts say using your EV's cruise control, autopilot and/or eco mode can help avoid peaks and dips in acceleration that can drain your battery. If you're running low on charge during a long drive and you're not sure you'll make it to a charger, Mr Siem says "the best thing to do is actually just slow down". "Even from 100 [kilometres per hour] to 90 makes a big difference," he says. "If you really need to eke it out, then going down to 70 will actually give you a lot more range." Turning off your air con and other unnecessary add-ons can help too, but speed is "by far" the biggest drain, Mr Siem says. Tyre pressure, weight and aerodynamic drag Outside of speed, tyre pressure is probably the biggest drain on EV charge, Mr Siem says. "[If] tyres are significantly deflated … they will produce a lot of drag; they won't roll as efficiently, so they will use a lot more energy," he says. He recommends keeping them to the manufacturer's recommended pressure and checking them once a month. Keeping your tyre pressure at the manufacturer's recommended level will reduce rolling drag and battery drain. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Jessica Hinchliffe ) Mr Martin says avoiding excess weight and aerodynamic drag can also help. "The more … you're carrying around, the more energy you're using," he says. "Make sure you're not carrying around things that you don't need." He says anything that adds drag, like roof racks, also drains power. Preserving battery life and charging cheaply Treating your battery well is another way to help preserve your range in the longer term. "Batteries nowadays are pretty capable, so as long as you're sensible … they'll actually last really well," Mr Day says.

events.title: The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly | Editorial
events.summary: Bill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failure This month, a cross-party parliamentary committee said Thames Water should be placed in temporary state control and that any takeover by its creditors should be halted. The MPs were right. The “ special administration ” regime keeps the taps running while shareholders are wiped out, creditors take a haircut and the firm’s £19bn of debt is restructured. But it must not then be handed back to private hands. After Thames Water has failed its 16 million customers, polluted rivers , paid out billions to shareholders and repeatedly demanded higher bills, a City-friendly reprieve would only reward the outrageous behaviour that the regulatory system is meant to deter. Ministers ought to seize the opportunity to nationalise Thames Water. In July, Andy Burnham agreed. On the campaign trail in Makerfield, he told reporters that “there’s a very strong case for public ownership [for Thames Water] to sort out its problems”. Having entered parliament and become prime minister, Mr Burnham is instead looking at letting elected mayors “ oversee ” private water companies. There is nothing wrong with more democratic scrutiny. However, oversight without ownership and proper control seems like a sleight of hand. Voices from different wings of the party recognise this. Mr Burnham can’t kick the decision down the road for ever. Continue reading...

events.title: Trump: 5 terrorism suspects in U.K. base incident were under investigation
events.summary: British police arrested five men Sunday on suspicion of terrorism near a U.K. air base used for U.S. operations in Iran , as President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation. The latest: "Working with Britain, it was an amazing job," Trump told reporters Sunday morning. "We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great and we got them." The big picture: Officials declared a major incident and set up roadblocks overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. The incident, which British investigators did not immediately link to Tehran , comes one day after Trump said he'd rejected the latest Iranian proposal to end the war — though he told Axios's Barak Ravid on Sunday that he expects fresh talks this week. State of play: Police received a call around 12.45 a.m. Sunday local time relating to "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be traveling towards the air base used by the U.S. 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron, per a Metropolitan Police statement . Armed officers responded in the area of Whelford, a village some 33 miles from the city of Oxford. There they arrested the men "on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act" and they were further arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act," according to the statement. Zoom in: U.K. counter-terrorism official Vicki Evans said officers established a 400-meter cordon (roughly a quarter-mile) around vehicles in the area while the British Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit conducted examinations. "As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place," she said in a statement. A nearby leisure centre was opened for people evacuated from the area. Context: RAF Fairford is the U.S. Air Force's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe and supports a variety of missions and exercises throughout the year, according to the Air Force. Flashback: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned in July that any base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target" in a statement that specifically referenced U.S. B-1 bombers flying from RAF Fairford. What they're saying: The 501st Combat Support Wing told Axios that no U.S. Air Force personnel were involved in the incident. "The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," the statement said. "We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities." Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

events.title: Armani's business and creative evolution on show in Milan a year after founder's death
events.summary: Giorgio Armani’s empire is taking shape a year after the designer’s death MILAN -- The future of Giorgio Armani ’s empire is coming into sharper focus a year after the designer’s death. On the runway in Milan, his signature elegance defined the latest collection previewed on Sunday, while behind the scenes talks are set to begin on the sale of a stake, as stipulated in his will. Armani gave preference to LVMH, L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica as potential buyers of a 15% stake to be sold within 18 months of his death on Sept. 4, 2025, at the age of 91. Chief Executive Giuseppe Marsocci told reporters backstage at the runway show that there were no favorites and that the stake could potentially be split among all three companies. “It is not written in stone that there has to be one,” he said. Marsocci said the will allowed discussions to begin only after the first anniversary of Armani’s death but declined to confirm whether they had started. “The assumption” that talks were underway “may have some logic,” he said. The recent appointment of Dario Vitale as head of accessories at Giorgio Armani and creative director of Emporio Armani has generated interest in the fashion house’s creative future. No date has been announced for his runway debut. Asked whether Vitale’s role could expand, Marsocci said everything was evolving. “From here into the future, you never know,” he said. IRGC will target US ships in Indian Ocean if fighting resumes, official says District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' White House orders over $800M in funds rescinded The womenswear collection for next spring and summer deliberately mixed daywear with evening looks, with sparkle running through both. Lean, fluid trousers and long dresses shaped the silhouette, often paired with rigid bodices. The collection was titled “Evolution.” “It evolved in the sense that it is fashion that everyone can wear,” said Silvana Armani, the late designer’s niece and longtime head of womenswear. She departed from her uncle’s legacy in one important way: incorporating cotton, a textile that she said he didn’t like but which she “adores.” The designer’s presence was most felt in the collection in two pieces: a recreation of the formal double-breasted Communion suit that Armani wore when he was 8-years-old and a graphic jacket bearing his smiling image. events.summary: President Trump plans to host Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at a private White House dinner on Sunday evening, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The dinner —the first one-on-one meeting between the two— is an indication of thawing relations between Anthropic and the administration, whose officials and allies have had longstanding tensions. Driving the news: Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson plan to meet top AI CEOs Tuesday at the White House, and this friendly dinner serves as an appetizer. Top tech CEOs from OpenAI's Sam Altman to Google's Sundar Pichai flanked Trump during a state dinner last week but there was one notable exception —Amodei, who had a scheduling conflict. Afterward, Trump personally invited Amodei to the dinner, one of the sources said. The big picture: Anthropic's relationship with the administration has been on shaky ground all year, with signs of warming quickly deteriorating thereafter. Between the lines: Amodei is such a quirky and controversial figure in AI that he has started to enter mainstream pop culture. Amodei was mocked on the latest episode of Saturday Night Live over his personality traits and his views on AI safety. Last week, Trump allies circulated talking points to the White House that emphasized Amodei's role in, and the oddities of, the effective altruism movement . Months ago, when Anthropic first started talking about having a one-on-one with Trump, some advised against it because "Dario's a little too weird" for Trump, one senior official told Axios. What they are saying: "President Trump has been clear: America will lead the world in Super Intelligence, while protecting American consumers," a White House official said. "We will drive innovation, strengthen American competitiveness, and ensure this transformative technology works for the American people." The bottom line: In an administration that is so closely attuned to the president's moods and personal relationships, a sit down with Trump at the White House is priceless for any company.

events.title: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week
events.summary: One day after he rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war, President Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he expects U.S. negotiators to engage in more talks with the country this week. Why it matters: Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, but the two sides are far apart on the key issues. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration is demanding that Iran agree to nuclear concessions. Two regional sources confirmed Trump's comment about more talks this week. They said they expect another round of indirect dialogue between the U.S. and Iran as early as Monday. But it isn't clear if the gaps can be bridged. What he's saying: "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said. Asked if he is considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump said: "I am always thinking about it." State of play: In the meantime, Trump said, the U.S. military is facilitating a lot of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. He said that over the weekend the largest amount of oil transited through the strait since the war began. "More than 20 million barrels," Trump said. A U.S. defense official confirmed Trump's assertion, saying that on Friday night 22 million barrels of oil were exported through the strait. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last Tuesday. Qatari officials participated, passing messages between the two sides. Araghchi delivered to Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and restarting nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. Trump rejected the Iranian proposal on Saturday. Behind the scenes: But a U.S. official and two regional sources told Axios that Qatari mediators are continuing shuttle diplomacy to try to reach a deal. On Thursday, the prime minister of Qatar met in New York with the Iranian president and discussed the potential deal with the Trump administration. Shortly after, senior Qatari officials met Witkoff and briefed him. A regional source with knowledge of the indirect negotiations said the Qatari mediators discussed the original Iranian proposal with both parties and provided a compromise proposal to both sides to review. What to watch: Over the weekend, the Qatari mediators have been going back and forth separately with Iranian and U.S. negotiators on changes to the text. Qatari mediators are expected to meet separately with Araghchi and Witkoff as early as Monday. The other side: Araghchi told NBC on Sunday that despite Trump's rejection of the Iranian proposal, Iran still wants a diplomatic solution. He said that the midterm elections aren't part of Iran's calculations. "We only care about our national interests. We are ready for negotiations," he said. "Although we heard from President Trump that he's rejecting this deal ... we are still waiting for an official response through the mediators," Araghchi added.

events.title: Why the US-Iran war is working in China’s favour
events.summary: It must be unique for New York to host the president of a country at war with the US. But alongside Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian, who is in town for the UN General Assembly , an even more important protagonist in the conflict visited Donald Trump: Chinese leader Xi Jinping . What does Beijing stand to gain from the US-Iran conflict ? It benefits from Washington’s distraction. While a third of the US Navy is occupied in a war with no clear end goal, the US squanders munitions and international respect alike. Meanwhile, China is free to expand its strength, deal with its own problems and pose as the responsible, rule-abiding superpower. The current “warm war” suits it just fine. With a strenuous and expensive US military effort, oil and other commodities are getting out of the Gulf in increasing amounts, although not to pre-conflict levels. That keeps up the domestic political pressure on the White House and means it cannot easily walk away. China has reportedly provided satellite imagery to the Iranians to help them target US bases. It has also supplied shipments with dual-use components that Iran could use to build missiles and drones. As with Russia’s war against Ukraine, China can simultaneously profit, make itself invaluable to a combatant, keep a conflict bubbling along, restrain full-scale escalation and maintain the facade of benevolent neutrality. In this vein, China does not want energy flows from the Gulf to be almost entirely cut, or for Iran to escalate, or return to large-scale, damaging attacks against regional infrastructure, as in March and April. It is a key investor across the Arab Gulf countries, much more than in Iran. It has large and expensive assets and many of its citizens live in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and Iraq. The Bab Al Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, under recent threat from Iran’s allies, the Houthis in Yemen, is a key conduit for Chinese goods to Europe. A Chinese naval base in Djibouti keeps watch over this strait. The GCC and Iraq are cumulatively far more important energy suppliers, customers and economic partners for China than Iran. Beijing does not need to choose between them. In 2023, it brokered a deal to restore diplomatic relations between Riyadh and Tehran, following the damaging drone and missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities in 2019. Some hoped it would intervene to prevent a repeat. In this year’s war, China might have quietly restrained Iran from trying to unleash more devastation on Saudi energy infrastructure, which would damage its own interests, but it has not emerged as a mediator. Staying out of the morass probably seems wise in Beijing now, though it does impose a hard limit on China’s diplomatic and security weight. It has to be careful not to appear a fair-weather friend, or worse, a two-faced one, in the Gulf. A return to the near-total blockade seen early in the war would hurt China’s key trading partners in Asia and Europe, notably energy-short Japan, South Korea and the Asean nations. Its export-dependent economy is limping; it does not want a global recession. But Beijing is the best-prepared major nation for such an energy crisis, if it continues at a restrained level. Unlike the US, now a major net exporter, it is the world’s largest importer of both oil and gas. However, its domestic coal resource base and its vast and growing renewable and nuclear sectors insulate its electricity system from gas shocks. It can be relatively flexible in its imports of liquefied natural gas, where Qatari shipments have been severely disrupted, because of its major gas pipelines from Russia and Central Asia. In turn, Moscow’s decision to torpedo its core European gas market has left it reliant on its giant eastern neighbour. Another ill-judged decision to go to war has contributed to Chinese ascendancy. Last year, almost as if Beijing foresaw what was coming, it accumulated huge strategic stocks of oil, which it has been gradually drawing down since the start of the war. Its state-directed energy system has proven a useful tool in meeting national priorities. It continues to electrify its road transport, gradually reducing its need for petroleum. And its juggernaut of a clean-tech sector continues to gain from the war. Six of the top seven electric vehicle makers worldwide are Chinese. It accounts for about 79 per cent of the world’s wind turbine market, 80 per cent of the global solar photovoltaic market, and 80 to 90 per cent of core components for lithium-ion batteries. Independent Chinese refiners did benefit from the opportunity to import cut-price Iranian crude. With the effective US maritime blockade, the last dribs of that are arriving. We still have to see whether China will help its friend weather the embargo, or somehow enable more Iranian oil to evade the stranglehold. After losing an ally in Venezuela in January, it will not want to see another leading oil exporter forced to bow to America. On August 24, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “Economic D-Day” against Iran. But notably, the tougher sanctions have not specifically targeted China, which remains Tehran’s key trading partner and essentially the only remaining customer for its oil. Some previous American measures have hit individual Chinese independent refineries and oil terminals, but none of the major or systemically important ones. China has enacted counter-sanctions, which would target companies complying with US restrictions, presenting them with a tricky choice. This resembles the European Union’s blocking statute, first introduced in 1996 and revived in 2018. But Brussels has never had the guts to wield this weapon seriously; Beijing will. It has leverage over the US, particularly in its ability to cut off rare-earth supplies. China thus has significant influence over the success of American sanctions against both Tehran and Moscow. Of course, things could still go wrong. Chinese petroleum stocks are not infinite, while the US’s mastery of shale oil and gas remains a huge strategic advantage. A breakthrough in nuclear fusion or artificial intelligence might turbocharge the US energy system. The regime in Tehran could collapse under the strains of war and sanctions, and hand the US another invaluable Middle Eastern ally. For all its strengths, China’s state-centric economy has serious long-term weaknesses. It cannot shrug off a severe shortage of oil indefinitely, in combination with its huge debt overhang, a real estate slump, an ageing workforce, and an over-reliance on exports in a suspicious world. Yet, as US secretary of state Madeleine Albright said in 1998, “We are the indispensable nation. We stand tall, and we see further than other countries into the future.” Now she might have been speaking from the Great Hall of the People by Tiananmen Square.

events.title: The most pressing midterm issues for rural voters
events.summary: Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Cost of living and health care costs top the list of issues rural voters want 2026 midterm candidates to address, according to a new AP/KFF poll . The big picture: Ahead of the midterms, rural voters rank pocketbook concerns above immigration, the conflict with Iran and several major domestic policy debates. By the numbers: 69% of rural voters said it is 'extremely important' for candidates to talk about the cost of living, followed by health care costs (56%) and fraud in government programs (54%). Context: The AP/KFF poll asked 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas how important it was for 2026 candidates to talk about each of eight issues. Cost of living concerns Zoom in: Affordability concerns extend across a wide range of everyday expenses. 57% of rural voters cited an economic concern — including rising costs, jobs, wages and housing affordability — when asked about the biggest issue facing their local community. 67% said they were at least somewhat worried about affording gas or transportation, while 66% said the same about health care and 60% about food and groceries. Three-quarters rated the cost of living in their area as either "fair" or "poor," up 25 percentage points from 2017. Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Reality check: Rural voters' unhappiness with costs doesn't necessarily translate into support for Democrats. According to the poll, 40% trust Republicans more to handle the cost of living, compared with 25% who trust Democrats and 27% who trust neither party. Rural voters in the survey leaned Republican: 54% identified as GOP voters or Republican-leaning independents, while 32% identified as Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents. What we're watching: Whether economic frustration affects voter enthusiasm among rural Republicans. 27% of rural Republican voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, per the poll. Among them, 59% say they're absolutely certain to vote in the midterms. Still, 98% of rural Republicans say they're more likely to vote for a Republican than a Democrat. The fine print: The KFF/AP poll surveyed 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas nationwide from Aug. 12-24, 2026, online and by phone. The margin of sampling error is ±3 percentage points.

events.title: Namibia's president eyes local mineral processing
events.summary: The News Namibia’s president has a message for foreign investors eyeing the country’s critical minerals: build processing plants at home, or look elsewhere. “When you are coming to Namibia, you don’t want to be a briefcase business,” Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor at an Invest Africa event on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week. “You have to put up a processing plant in our country.” Namibia is a mining-based economy, she said, whose minerals have for too long been exported raw and shipped back as finished goods. The country is a major uranium producer with deposits of lithium, rare earths, copper and graphite. In exchange for processing at home, she offered investors a long-term partnership and a stable place to do business, pointing to 36 years of peace since independence. She also wants foreign firms to team up with local entrepreneurs, “so that you become part and parcel of us.” Her pitch reflects a hardening line across the continent. With demand for critical minerals surging and Washington and Beijing competing for supply, African governments are betting they have the leverage to demand more than royalties. About a dozen countries, including Guinea, Malawi and Zimbabwe, have restricted exports of unprocessed minerals to force local refining, borrowing from Indonesia’s nickel playbook. The goal is to capture more of the value chain, and the jobs that come with it, rather than remain suppliers of raw inputs for other countries’ industries. Know More Nandi-Ndaitwah is also going further than many peers on ownership. Asked whether local partnership would be mandatory for foreign investors, she told Semafor: “In fact, we are putting it in the law.” That promise has a long history. Namibia’s empowerment framework won cabinet approval in 2015 and was meant to become law by 2018. It stalled over a clause forcing businesses owned by previously advantaged Namibians to cede 25% to previously disadvantaged citizens, which was dropped in 2018. Business groups also warned it would scare off foreign investment. As recently as last October, officials described the bill as at an “advanced stage.” Mining is moving faster. Namibia has required 15% local ownership for new mining licenses since 2021. Officials floated a 51% threshold last year, drawing pushback from the Chamber of Mines, which warned against importing other countries’ models. Nandi-Ndaitwah dismissed comparisons with South Africa’s empowerment rules, saying it depends on the approach. She cited tourism conservancies she oversaw as environment minister. There, investors started with 60% to 70% stakes that stepped down to roughly 51-49 with local communities. Step Back Behind the hard line is a jobs emergency. “Over 40% of our people are unemployed. And we are sitting on a time bomb,” Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor. “Even when you have your mine there, it’s not safe.” Nandi-Ndaitwah won the presidency in 2024 on a pledge to spend 85 billion Namibian dollars (about $5 billion) creating 500,000 jobs by 2029, a steep target for a country of 3 million people with a GDP of about $14 billion. She framed the stakes in continental terms: without opportunity at home, young Africans will keep leaving. “If they have to leave, it is by choice,” she said. “But as it stands now, they are pushed out by the conditions in the continent.” Offshore oil discoveries could bankroll her jobs promise, or deepen the sense that Namibia’s wealth flows elsewhere.

events.title: China and US agree to tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods and AI dialogue
events.summary: The US and China have ​agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on artificial intelligence, the countries said ⁠following President Xi Jinping's visit to the US. The tariff reductions will apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said. “The ⁠two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods ​in each ⁠direction,” the White House said. The ‌three-day summit between Mr Xi and US President Donald Trump , which ended on Friday, was largely an exercise in mutual diplomacy but did feature some breakthroughs. The two sides agreed to set up a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said. The agreement follows a move by the world's two largest economies to extend a trade truce that had been due to expire on November 10 by two months, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “This historic visit enriched the constructive and stable China-US relationship, upheld the overall stability of bilateral ties, opened a new chapter in China-US relations, and will have a far-reaching impact on world peace and development,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said. 'Super intelligence' On AI, the ​two sides agreed to hold dialogue on the technology's risks and ‌benefits, with the next round of discussions ⁠set for November, and to set up ​a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said. The ​White House ‌said the leaders had agreed to use the term “super intelligence” in place of “artificial intelligence”. The ⁠Chinese Ministry said Beijing valued Washington's use of the new term. As AI technology continues ⁠to advance, the two sides should step up exchanges and work towards consensus in line with new developments, the statement said. The US and China also agreed to support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation leaders' meeting and the Group of 20 summit, with both leaders planning to attend the gatherings ​hosted by the other. On foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran should fulfil its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways.
