events.title: It's a 5% world. We're just living in it
events.summary: The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher , with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook. The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%. Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption. It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades. Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over. Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government. While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last. Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance. Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation. Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative. The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages. State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans. Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000. Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up. People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust. The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier. The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained. By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills. But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that. In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline. Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time. So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump). The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital. And that adjustment is in its early days.

events.title: Apple buried Copland 30 years ago. Now the failed OS boots in a browser
events.summary: Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil, also known as Mist, made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator. Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference, but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation. There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin, but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody, followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8, released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release. Further pieces of Copland's work appeared across Mac OS 8 and 9, allowing Apple to improve the old platform while Mac OS X was being prepared. When Apple bought NeXT, NeXTSTEP already ran on Motorola 680x0, Intel x86, Sun SPARC and HP PA-RISC processors. That portable foundation later helped Apple move the Mac to Intel, while OS X became the basis for the operating systems used by the iPhone and iPad. Apple's future might have looked very different had Copland succeeded. Now it's easier than ever to see why it didn't. ®

events.title: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
events.summary: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." events.title: A tradie tipped this suburb off on a new data centre build. Residents are furious
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Suburban residents protest 15-metre power poles linked to data centre expansion Topic: Urban Development and Planning Industrial power poles 15 metres high have been installed outside Cameron Botterill's house. ( ABC News ) When Cameron Botterill left home one morning, he didn't expect to return to 15-metre power poles soaring above his residential street in Melbourne's inner west. "They're absolute monstrosities," Mr Botterill said. "They're ginormous. They tower above anything else in the suburb and they look very industrial. We're in a residential area here and we definitely did not ask for them to be installed." The power poles went up within a day. ( ABC News ) The new poles are more than twice the height of the 7-metre wooden poles they replaced, and can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, roughly 160 times the voltage that previously ran through his street. In July, Mr Botterill was notified by his electricity distributor, Jemena, that the power would be shut off to allow workers to replace the poles on his street. He didn't find out why until the day the new poles appeared. "I was shocked that this could be installed in a residential area." The site of the NextDC data centre in West Footscray. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The NextDC data centre in nearby West Footscray is already operating, and it's being expanded. One more data centre is proposed for the suburb with another in Spotswood. Jemena says the new power poles are part of its local network upgrade "to help support Melbourne's growing energy needs". "These taller power poles are required mainly for safety reasons," said Michael Brear, a mechanical engineering professor at the University of Melbourne. "When you have a large electrical load like a data centre, you supply it most economically at a higher voltage than typically you would in your home. On streets where the poles have been installed in Melbourne's inner west, there is a strikingly consistent complaint: residents didn't know the change was happening. The power levels required for data centres mean old 7-metre wooden poles have to be replaced. ( ABC News ) In response to questions from 7.30, Jemena said: "We have heard feedback from residents and other stakeholders that our communication and engagement could have been better, and we are taking that feedback seriously." The company told 7.30 it has "paused works and [is] taking the time to listen to the community to understand their concerns". Paul Tyndale was one of those caught by surprise when Jemena crews disconnected his power in the inner west suburb of Spotswood to install a new taller pole. It was only then his family found out a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away. Paul Tyndale found out from a tradie that a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away from his home. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "We found out about the data centre when the tradie who was disconnecting our house told my partner, 'This is for the new data centre,'" he said. GreenSquare, the company behind the proposed Spotswood Data Centre, now states on its website that the Spotswood poles are not part of its proposal and "are separate electricity network infrastructure works". On Sanderson Street in Yarraville, residents decided to fight back. After neighbours saw 15-metre poles go up a few blocks over, they knew their block was next. Residents on Sanderson Street saw the 15-metre poles going up nearby. ( Supplied ) On the day Jemena crews showed up in August, residents left cars and bins out to block equipment needed to install the poles. Some taped notes on car windows explaining the protest action. Residents on Sanderson Street left cars out to block the equipment needed to install the poles. ( Supplied ) "We were all just really caught off guard and just felt like it was really unfair that we weren't told about what was happening," resident Katrina Dardha said. Eventually, unable to get their equipment in position, the crews filled in the holes they had prepared for upgraded power poles and left. Milco Bogoevski (second from the right) and his neighbours staged a protest to stop the power poles from going up in their street. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "Everyone decided this is not happening on our watch," resident Milco Bogoevski said. "If you stay quiet, it's at your own peril. I guess sometimes it takes something to make you really angry, to make you stand up." State Labor MP Katie Hall's seat includes West Footscray, home to a large NextDC data centre.

events.summary: In the first article in a series on the Polish economy, we look at the country’s defence boom and its implications A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów. events.title: UAE remains magnet for ultra-wealthy undeterred by war disruption
events.summary: Old money is staying put and the flow of new wealth to the UAE continues, despite naysayers fearing war-driven risks and uncertainties. The Emirates' appeal to the ultra-wealthy remains firm as the benefits, beyond just the lifestyle and security, of relocating to the Arab world’s second-largest economy far outweigh potential risks, wealth managers say. Close to 10,000 millionaires were estimated to have moved to the UAE in 2025 and thousands more were expected to relocate this year. Many may choose not to do so because of the US-Iran war's impact on the region, but it is not correct to say the conflict has completely reversed the relocation trend, private bankers serving the UAE's uber-rich say. Global banks such as HSBC and DBS, South-East Asia's biggest lender by assets with headquarters in Singapore, are investing heavily in building their wealth offerings and have not stopped hiring private bankers to better serve their clientele. Although sentiment does play a part, entrepreneurs, high-net-worth individuals, family offices and institutional wealth have a longer-term view. They look at fundamentals as well as the structural strengths and regulatory make-up of a destination before making a relocation decision. “In our client conversations, the UAE's appeal remains firmly in view despite the conflict,” says Aladdin Hangari, HSBC's head of global private banking for the Middle East and North Africa. “The reasons people came – stability, safety, a clear tax and residency framework, and world-class connectivity – are structural, not sentiment.” The conversations that British lender Barclays’ wealth managers are having with their clientele are no different, indicating a strong conviction in the UAE's value proposition. “Families and entrepreneurs are drawn here because of its economics … regulatory credibility, international outlook and ability to connect regional opportunities with global capital,” Farzad Billimoria, head of Barclays Private Bank in the UAE, says. “Those attributes remain firmly intact.” While recent events have brought resilience and risk management into focus, they have also reinforced the importance of jurisdictions that offer “stability, clarity and connectivity” rather than diminishing their attractiveness. “While sentiment can fluctuate in the short term, the factors underpinning the UAE’s appeal remain structural rather than cyclical,” Mr Billimoria says. Good numbers Wealthy individuals and family offices as well institutional investors are still arriving in good numbers from Europe and the UK. Affluent clients in South Asian economies, increasingly from East Asia and even from the wider Gulf region, have also chosen to relocate to the UAE in recent quarters, HSBC says. “The draw is consistent: stability, personal safety, no personal income tax, strong residency options, and a maturing family-office framework in DIFC and ADGM,” Mr Hangari says. “For many, the UAE is also a bridge to interests across Asia, Europe and Africa.” The UAE, one of the fastest-growing commercial and financial hubs in the Middle East, is a bridge between the fast-developing eastern economies and mature markets in the West. The seamless connectivity through Abu Dhabi and Dubai's aviation hubs as well as progressive regulatory regimes of the two emirates' respective onshore financial centres – ADGM and DIFC – position the hydrocarbons-rich country at the heart of global trade and commerce. Government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote workers, expansion of the 10-year Golden Visa programme and strong economic growth have also added to the Emirates’ appeal for the affluent. Migration hotspot Before the war broke out on February 28, the UAE was regarded as the migration hotspot for the ultra-wealthy as global millionaires sought to get away from established wealth centres to avoid heavy-handed changes in taxation regimes. Both Dubai and Abu Dhabi were ranked among the world’s top five destinations for entrepreneurs and high-net-worth investors. Dubai topped the charts with Abu Dhabi in fifth position, according to a survey by global property consultancy Savills. New York was second, Singapore third and Hong Kong fourth on the Savills HNWI Hotspot Index released in November last year. It analysed nearly 100 cities for business environment, family infrastructure and cost, legacy planning, lifestyle and privacy. A record 9,800 millionaires were estimated to have relocated in 2025 to the UAE amid a shake-up of financial regulations in London and growing scrutiny of the affluent elsewhere, according to the Wealth Migration Report 2025 by advisory Henley & Partners and wealth intelligence firm New World Wealth. In 2024, Dubai had an estimated population of 81,200 millionaires and 20 billionaires. Record quarterly growth in property prices in the emirate, especially the steep rise in sales of $10 million-plus uber-luxury residences before the US-Iran war jolted the global economy, was a reflection of the individual, family and institutional wealth the emirate has attracted in the past few years. Three large beachfront plots on an exclusive Dubai island were sold for an aggregate value of Dh1 billion ($272 million) between April and June this year, signalling that ultra-wealthy investors’ interest remains firm despite the Iran war. Sticky wealth While substantial new wealth flows continue despite geopolitical headwinds and extreme volatility in the oil markets, the outflow of capital was also not as significant as some analysts had anticipated during the early days of the conflict. “I would take the other side of the coin, which is how many people have left … how many families have decided to go back to the UK or to go back to France,” Loic Voide, head of private banking for the Middle East and Africa at DBS Bank, says. “It's not that much.” Julius Baer, the Swiss private bank, which manages close $550 billion in client assets, says having operated in the Middle East for over two decades, it has "consistently witnessed structural resilience rather than retreat". "Far from pulling back, our clients, especially UHNWIs and family offices have anchored their futures here," Rahul Malhotra, member of the Julius Baer's global wealth management committee and head of emerging markets says. "They are looking at the current environment with cautious optimism, keeping their focus firmly on long-term wealth preservation and legacy planning." HSBC’s Mr Hangari says “established wealth is sticky” and decisions to relocate homes, schooling, businesses or banking relationships are not dictated by short-term shocks. “If anything, more clients have deepened their ties to the UAE over the past five years,” he says. “What we hear is a decision to stay, and often to expand, and what keeps them is what brought them: a stable, predictable environment, personal safety, and an efficient base.” Barclays' Mr Billimoria agrees, saying for many of the wealthy individuals as well a

events.title: Small businesses under pressure as Canberrans weigh up cost of living
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACT small businesses vulnerable to rising cost of staying open as consumers weigh up living expenses Canberra's peak body for businesses fears the retail and hospitality sectors are the most vulnerable to increasing costs. ( ABC News: Elise Pianegonda ) The Canberra Business Chamber says small businesses will likely be the hardest hit by RBA interest rate hikes, along with property rate increases in Canberra. It comes as consumers are spending less, with some resorting to giving up their pets to animal shelters due to unaffordability. The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise interest rates next week to manage inflation. The CEO of the Canberra Business Chamber is confident when he says business sentiment in the territory is currently "as bad as it's ever been". The Reserve Bank is expected to raise interest rates a fourth time this year to manage inflation, in part from high fuel prices spurred on by the war in the Middle East, along with Australia's tight jobs market. At the moment, Canberrans are copping the highest fuel prices of all Australian capital cities. Canberra Business Chamber CEO Greg Harford said businesses felt pressure was mounting when simultaneously, consumers were not spending as much. "The cost of running a business is up, just as the cost of running a household is up," Mr Harford said. Canberra is currently the most expensive capital city in the country for both petrol and diesel. ( ABC News: Tahlia Roy ) "So there's less money coming in the door for many businesses, and that obviously puts real pressure on profitability in some of those areas." Retail, hospitality, services hardest hit Mr Harford said the coming expansion of portable long service leave to the hospitality and retail sector, while benefiting employees, was an example of rising costs which could ultimately be passed onto consumers. Under the portable long service scheme, casual workers have access to long service entitlements, even if they switch employers. Employers register and pay a set levy on the gross ordinary wages of eligible employees. Greg Harford says business sentiment is the worst he has seen. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Mr Harford also said Canberra's commercial property rates had gone up about 8 per cent this year. "My real worry is for those small businesses that are heavily leveraged, they've got very small margins, they're very reliant on customers coming through the door and spending, and those are the ones that are most at risk in the current situation," he said. Animal shelters around the country have been under strain as Australians weigh up living expenses with the cost of companion animals. The RSPCA says it is common for people to give up their pets to manage daily living costs. ( ABC News: Caitlin Maloney ) In the ACT since 2022, the cost of living has been one of the main reasons Canberrans were handing in their companion animals, according to the RSPCA. "'Unable to afford care' was the seventh most common surrender reason in FY22, but it has consistently ranked among the highest reasons in more recent years, including being the second most common reason for the past two years," Canberra's local RSPCA said.

events.title: Scoop: "Delusional" Senate forecast rattles Sea Island retreat
events.summary: A pollster for Senate Republicans was met with disbelief on Saturday after telling GOP donors and operatives that they could grow their majority in November's midterm elections , sources tell Axios. Why it matters : "Delusional," one attendee at the National Republican Senatorial Committee's Sea Island retreat in Georgia told Axios after the presentation by the pollster, Erik Iverson. "The mood is not good," said another. "I think most attendees down here are politically astute and realistic about the headwinds Republicans face," said a third. A fourth attendee described conversations at the event as Republicans sarcastically telling each other "we're winning" and "everything's good." The Sea Island fall retreat is a major donor event for the NRSC each cycle, attracting big-dollar donors, senators and their senior staff. The details : Iverson, a former Montana Republican Party chair, suggested that Republicans could net gain one seat in the Senate after the midterms, but did not provide a state-by-state explanation for how they would do so, sources said. Another source in the room said Iverson's comments were in the context of a question about the 2022 midterms, when Senate Democrats picked up a seat despite former President Biden's poor polling numbers. Some in the room laughed when a member of the audience asked if it meant Republicans would also pick up a seat, the source said. What he's saying: "I told attendees that I think all incumbent Republican Senators will hold their seats because we have good candidates who are well funded," Iverson told Axios. "And I pointed out that in 2022 President Biden's image was double digits under water in every single swing Senate seat yet Democrats still gained a seat. The message was for folks to keep their heads up," he added. Iverson presented polling findings on gas prices and data centers at a separate event earlier last week, according to slides obtained by Axios. It included that 60% of swing voters would consider supporting new data centers in their state if they met community requirements such as paying all their energy costs and not negatively affecting local water supplies. Between the lines : Attendees questioned why they were not given a full update on each race. The surprisingly competitive Texas race was not discussed at all, some sources noted. Zoom in: Other speakers on Saturday included NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.), Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W. Va.), Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and NRSC political director Brendan Jaspers. There was also a panel with Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Senate candidates Julia Letlow (Louisiana), Kevin Hern (Oklahoma), Andy Barr (Kentucky) and Harriet Hageman (Wyoming). The big picture : Top Senate Republicans openly acknowledge they face a tough map in November . Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told Axios on Wednesday that it's a "tough environment." The NRSC itself is asking donors for $9 million to help in three states — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio — where President Trump won by double digits in 2024, as Axios scooped on Thursday. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that Iverson presented polling findings on gas prices and data centers at a separate event earlier last week (not at the Sea Island event on Saturday).

events.title: Former vineyard turned into sanctuary for nationally threatened birds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts From vines to vegetation, property becomes safe haven for threatened bird species Tony and Cherie say they would recommend restoring land back to native vegetation to anyone considering removing vineyards. ( ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne ) A property in South Australia's Riverland region previously home to 40 acres of vineyards has been restored to native vegetation. The project has provided a sanctuary for the nationally threatened regent parrot. Vines continue to be ripped up across the region with the wine industry in crisis, but it is hoped the project could inspire others to do the same. On the banks of the River Murray in South Australia once lay rows of wine grapevines as far as the eye could see. In the middle of Australia's largest wine grape growing region at Murtho in the Riverland, Tony and Cherie Townsend's property is one of many that have ripped vines out of the ground. Rather than replace 40 acres of vines with another crop, in 2022 the pair decided to return their property to native vegetation. "It was a lot of time and effort [managing vineyards] and it wasn't the reason we bought the property in the first place," Ms Townsend said. Cherie and Tony Townsend say they are grateful for the opportunity to leave their property in a better place than they found it. ( ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne ) The decision to revitalise the riverfront property was an easy one for Ms Townsend, but she recognised the fortunate situation they were in to be able to make such a sacrifice compared to others nearby. "The decision to remove the vines was probably not as hard as what it has been for some other local growers," she said. Her 61-year-old husband said one of the driving factors in returning the site to native vegetation, rather than transitioning to another crop, was the potential return of the nationally threatened regent parrot. Flowers are blooming four years into the restoration project at the Townsends' property. ( ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne ) The pair said they would not have been able to do it on their own and have collaborated with the Murraylands and Riverland Landscape Board in bringing the site to life. The Townsends' property was identified as close to the perfect site for regent parrots, sitting right along a flight path for the eye catching native bird. There are extensive efforts across the Riverland to help the regent parrot. ( Supplied: Sputnik ) Regent parrot numbers have been in decline for several years, with a lack of available nesting sites part of the population problem. In its most recent census, the Landscape Board only recorded 400 breeding pairs of regent parrots in the Riverland. It is a number they are desperate to see rise during ongoing monitoring of the parrots, during the parrot's breeding season between August and November. "With regent parrots … anything we can do to restore and return land back to its natural form is amazing," threatened fauna ecologist Melissa Burford said. Mel Burford has been undertaking regent parrot surveying in recent weeks. ( ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne ) "They breed along the river corridor in the river red gums, but they forage in the mallee, so having that forage food available for them is really important." The South Australian Regent Parrot Recovery Team has also been consulted in the best way to attract the parrots and boost populations. Chair Kevin Smith has been surveying the parrots for 35 years and said populations had remained steady in recent years. He said the Townsends' property was so far the best example of native vegetation reintroduction helping the threatened species. Kevin Smith says regent parrots breed across a 200 kilometre stretch of the River Murray and backwaters in South Australia. ( ABC Riverland: Tom Nancarrow ) "It's very early stages but the regent parrots can get to their food source and not have to go through dangerous obstacles to get out to the mallee," Mr Townsend. Industry in crisis creates opportunity While the Townsends did not buy their current property for the purpose of growing wine grapevines, they have been involved in the industry since the late 1990s. It's meant they have a good understanding of the industry and its struggles in recent years . "We've done eight harvests here and after 2022 … pricing was heading south," Mr Townsend said. That is a feeling shared right across the Riverland, as the wine grape industry continues to battle an oversupply and a decline in wine consumption globally . The sight of grapevines being ripped out has become increasingly common across the Riverland.

events.title: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
events.summary: OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic, sources told Axios. Why it matters : The sheer number of incidents, which occurred in recent months in internal testing and the real world, indicates that the problem is orders of magnitude more complex than what is publicly known. The findings, which are surfacing as part of internal work to assess models and in investigations at both companies into model behavior, raise questions about whether either company — or any top model-maker — is currently capable of establishing complete control over their technology. The details : The episodes include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors, sources said. They occurred in internal testing and in the real world, and many have yet to become public as security researchers continue to investigate, sources said. Some of the testing is akin to "red-teaming" activity, where the companies are trying to get the models to misbehave in order to ensure that they are safe, sources said. Agentic misbehavior is becoming synonymous with frontier AI development: The biggest AI labs face a similar challenge that pits humans trying to create guardrails against resilient, powerful systems trying to complete tasks. Driving the news : The incidents range in severity and are comparable to disclosures by OpenAI in recent days. They include both successful attempts to bypass guardrails and unsuccessful ones, and most so far are not known to have caused real-world harm. The total could grow well beyond tens of thousands, sources said. In recent days, OpenAI and outside researchers have disclosed a litany of episodes involving model behavior from the company's systems that some experts consider troubling. These include OpenAI agents leaking 53 images from ChatGPT users online, the breach of an Australian government website , and attempts to hack other sites — including from the U.S. government — according to the company, sources and reports from Reuters and The New York Times . OpenAI announced it was pausing training on its most capable models and would resume training them "only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place," a spokesperson told Axios. Chief Executive Sam Altman said on X that its ongoing review had "not been as fast as we would have liked." Altman said the Hugging Face incident is the most severe they've seen. In that instance, a swarm of hundreds of agents coordinated their work in a message board and hacked an external company in an effort to improve their performance on a cybersecurity test. "People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves," an OpenAI spokesperson told Axios. "This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it will be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance." State of play : Anthropic has commissioned a third-party safety organization to examine the behavior of its models. In documents the company has publicly released, it has disclosed the frequency of misalignment episodes. The "system card" for its Opus 5.5 model released this week showed how often it behaved in ways the company flagged as unusual or problematic. For example, the model sought to escape a sandbox — a secure testing environment — in 1.5% of test runs, though the company emphasized that these were adversarial experiments where a task couldn't be solved without escaping the sandbox. Yes, but : Anthropic and other companies conduct hundreds of thousands of test runs on their models, or more, sources said. That means even a small percentage of misaligned behavior can still amount to tens of thousands of incidents in which the models behaved in unexpected, sometimes troubling ways. The Hugging Face incident , as well as a slew of others that have followed , led top AI executives to call for a slowdown in development and to ask for more robust federal and international regulations. Some at OpenAI see Hugging Face as a one-off, with disclosures about future incidents likely to be less severe due to improved controls and the unusual nature of the testing they conducted, which involved an unreleased model, sources told Axios. AI security researchers agree that there are simple fixes that will help AI companies avoid aspects of what made the Hugging Face episode appear so dangerous to outsiders. Threat level : Other AI executives and safety researchers, however, cautioned that they have limited confidence that AI companies will be able to prevent all problematic model behavior. The new crop of AI models complete tasks with extraordinary resilience, so working to limit their resourcefulness is often a losing game because it is necessary to anticipate every possible way they might run amok. Often, a technique that may have never occurred to humans is what allows them to slip past guardrails, top AI executives said. "Trying to come up with a perfect list of dos and don'ts is probably a fool's errand," one cybersecurity executive said. Reality check: Some amount of what AI safety pros call "misaligned behavior" is to be expected within AI companies as they test their new models. Bringing the risk of misalignment to zero may not be feasible, experts told Axios. Zoom in : The concern is if a model takes a problematic action many times in testing, it's more likely that model's behavior would cause a cyber incident in the real world. "What we have seen in terms of what these agents are up to is just the tip of the iceberg," researcher Conrad Stosz at Transluce, an independent AI evaluator, told Axios. It's not about how damaging each individual instance was, Connor Leahy, AI researcher and executive director at ControlAI told Axios. The "crazy thing," he said, is that these instances involve "autonomous systems doing things they were told not to do," potentially including crimes. The bottom line : Expect new disclosures about model misbehavior as AI companies continue to expand frontier capabilities.

events.title: Price hike could be offset with smaller pipes, water utility says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasWater suggests customers reduce pipe size to offset price hike, inquiry hears TasWater made changes to its fixed water and sewerage fees at the start of July. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Tasmanian businesses have slammed a TasWater suggestion to reduce pipe sizes to lower fixed water bills. TasWater says charges are calculated by the size of a property's water meter connection. Users say replacing meter connections could be costly. Tasmanian businesses have slammed a recommendation by the state's water utility encouraging customers affected by bill increases to reduce the size of their pipes. As of July, water bills for Tasmanian households and small businesses will rise by an average of 5.7 per cent each year for the next four years. Businesses and sports clubs said they have been hard hit by the changes, with some citing an increase of as much as 500 per cent to their fixed water bill. In a parliamentary inquiry into the financial and operational performance of TasWater on Thursday, representatives suggested one option to help reduce water bills for those affected would be to reduce meter connections to 20 millimetres in size. In the 2023–24 financial year, TasWater lost 24.5 per cent of its treated water. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) One local business said replacing pipes could cost as much as $100,000, with no guarantee that they could be reduced to 20 millimetres. TasWater has previously said that while the upfront cost would be several thousand dollars, the returns would be greater. Water bill increases surpass 500 per cent Co-director of Rocherlea steel fabricating business HP Engineering Stuart Boyd said the business's monthly water bill in June was $625, equivalent to $7,500 per year. Stuart Boyd says replacing TasWater pipes would be an involved process. ( Supplied ) After the changes, this increased by more than 500 per cent to $3,800 a month, or more than $45,000 a year. Mr Boyd said reducing the company's inward water pipes, which are 150 millimetres in size, could cost as much as $100,000. "We'd have to get engineers and more consultants to design and do a study," he said. "There'd be business disruptions to dig up from the road in and change pipe sizes. You're talking labour, materials, the cost of your building surveyor, there'd be design work involved." TasWater said it recognised the scale of the increase for some non-residential customers and was actively consulting with the economic regulator on other ways it could minimise impacts. TasWater has defended the price increase, saying funds are needed to upgrade its aging infrastructure. ( Supplied: Taswater ) TasWater Customer and Community General Manager Callan Paske explained the increased pricing, saying that "a larger water meter connection lets a property draw more water at any time than a standard home". "Our pipes, pumps, treatment plants and storages have to be built and maintained to meet that potential demand, whether it's used on a given day or not. "Fixed charges recover the cost of holding that capacity available." Customer impact assessed case-by-case Last year, TasWater applied to the state's economic regulator for an average price increase of 11.5 per cent per year to fixed sewerage and water fees, but the application was knocked back earlier this year. Calls for alert system to warn of sewage releases More than half a billion litres of improperly treated sewage were released into the state's waterways in the 2024 to 2025 financial year. TasWater has previously said its price increases were to fund necessary upgrades to aging water and sewerage infrastructure . Mr Paske said potential costs and savings varied depending on the property and the work involved in reducing the pipe sizes. "We'd encourage businesses to talk to us rather than assume a figure," he said. Mr Paske said affected customers would be assessed on a case-by-case basis. "It would need to be determined that a smaller connection can meet the property's ongoing water needs and applicable requirements. This involves a development application to TasWater and supporting information prepared by a suitably qualified surveyor or engineer," he said. Mr Boyd said his fabrication business would need to increase its prices to cover the additional costs. "We don't survive or operate in a way that we have contracts in place. We've got to compete, we've got to tender and we have to win work. So that would jeopardise, make it harder for us to win work," he said. Haylee Sheehan's furniture transport business in Youngtown, on the outskirts of Launceston, was also hit by a significant bill increase.

events.title: The residents and wind farm on the frontline of Australia's energy wars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mount Fox residents say they bear brunt of net zero as wind farm construction to begin The locality of Mount Fox was named after the iconic crater of an inactive 100,000-year-old volcano. ( Supplied: Keep Mount Fox Wild ) Construction will soon begin on the nation's largest wind farm to be built in two years, but frustrated residents say they are bearing the brunt of Australia's push for net zero. The Gawara Baya wind farm includes 68 turbines and a 100-megawatt battery spread over 148 hectares near the 100,000-year-old dormant volcano Mount Fox in north Queensland. Danish investors Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) acquired the project from WindLab earlier this month, announcing funding was ready and construction would begin "imminently". Energy experts say the development is a breakthrough towards the federal government's 2030 renewables goal. The 100,000-year-old dormant volcano Mount Fox rises from the surrounding bushland near Ingham. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Mount Fox near Ingham has about 84 residents and neighbours the world heritage listed Wet Tropics. There is a campground with a concrete cricket pitch, road signs warning motorists about cassowaries, and a primary school with a mob of emus and three students. "I wake up every morning and there's big trees and open spaces and all you hear is nature in all its diversity," resident Kim Armstrong said. Kim Armstrong is opposed to the windfarm development. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) The closest turbine will be about 5 kilometres from the Wet Tropics border. Ms Armstrong said she was worried about the impact of the 140-metre turbines on the region's biodiversity, human and environmental health, run-off onto the Great Barrier Reef and what would happen to the turbines after their 35-year life cycle. "I don't think a lot of Australians really understand exactly what it takes to put a wind farm up and the destruction that it causes," she said. A wind-powered relic at Mount Fox. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Ms Armstrong said Mount Fox residents were on the frontline of Australia's energy wars, pursuing the "dream" of net zero because of political decisions made 2,000 kilometres away in Canberra by people she did not vote for. She said people in cities thought "we have to do this for climate change" and resisting labelled her a "climate denier". "That's not the case at all," she said. Some Mount Fox residents say net zero is a dream ruining their idyllic home. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Ms Armstrong founded community group Keep Mount Fox Wild, which she said included about half of the town's residents. "There are several wind farms earmarked for up here. We just don't want them," she said. CIP project CEO Mark Branson said the project met strict government regulations. "We understand that not everybody in the region is a fan of wind farms and this is always the case," he said. A sign opposing wind turbines in the kitchenette of the Mount Fox campground. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) "But we know we have a really good foundation for the project in terms of the rigorous environmental assessment that has been done, all the community consultation that's been done, all the engagement with the local businesses and councils." He said construction would create about 500 jobs, with most workers to be housed at an onsite village. Mr Branson said Gawara Baya was paving the way for new wind projects to replace aging coal assets. "Projects like Gawara Baya are really critical in making sure we've got enough electricity to feed into the grid and power people's homes, to power industry and make sure we've got stable electricity supply into the future," he said. A map of the planned locations of the 68 windfarms near Mount Fox. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) This project is the first wind farm to reach construction under the federal government's Capacity Investment Scheme and represents a breaking of a deadlock, according to Grattan Institute climate and energy program director Alison Reeve. "The hope of the industry is that this project is a sign that that pipeline is finally moving and that this is going to be the first of quite a lot of projects, particularly on the east coast, that will now start to get built," Ms Reeve said. Alison Reeve says the Gawara Baya project is the biggest to reach financial close under the Capacity Investment Scheme. ( ABC News ) Under the scheme, which aims to help achieve the target of 82 per cent renewables by 2030, the government guarantees the price for electricity, subsidising the producer if electricity prices fall and sharing in profits if prices rise above a certain price.

events.title: This bar's renovations could be blueprint for disability-friendly venues
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney nightclub Club 77 redesigns venue with accessibility front of mind DJ Lana Zilla wishes there were more live music venues that catered to people who need greater accessibility. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) Lana Zilla has been a DJ in Sydney for the better part of 15 years, but lately, they have not been behind the decks as much. They have what they describe as "dynamic" or "fluctuating" disabilities, which means sometimes they require mobility aids such as a walker or a stick. "I haven't been DJ’ing, because it can be hard to ask for [accommodations]," they said. At the clubs they do play at, Mx Zilla said generally, accessibility was "not great". Dane Gorrel is the owner of Club 77 in Sydney's Darlinghurst. ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) It is an issue that has prompted Dane Gorrel, who owns Club 77 in Darlinghurst, to make some major changes. "We programmed some artists with disability a couple of times … and there was always issues with setting it up, and making it right, and making it comfortable for them," he said. "Making the club accessible has been something that we've been looking at for a very long time." The new DJ booth can be adjusted for a performers' height. ( ABC News ) The electronic music venue has been a fixture of the city's nightclubbing scene for almost three decades. Longtime patrons would be familiar with the steep set of stairs at its entry way, leading to a moody, tight techno basement. But earlier this year, it used a grant from the NSW government to undergo an extensive renovation. After months of work, Club 77 reopened in late July with a redesign focused on accessibility. The venue used a grant from the NSW government to undergo an extensive renovation. ( ABC News ) The club sought advice from an accessibility consultant and other members of the disabled and electronic music communities. The back-alley entrance has a ramp and a wheelchair lift, accessible bathrooms have been installed, part of the bar has been lowered, and there is a dedicated sensory area off the dance floor. The DJ booth can be adjusted for a performers' height, and can move forward and backward to accommodate mobility aids. Haptic vests, which vibrate to the beat of the music, are also available for patrons who are deaf or hard-of-hearing. Haptic vests are available for patrons who are deaf or hard-of-hearing. ( ABC News ) The more accessibility upgrades, 'the better' Interior designer Kristie Paul was brought onboard for the project. "I've been here probably about 400 times … so I was very happy to be involved," she said. "There was a lot of feasibility, a lot of research, a lot of investigation, numerous consultants and numerous iterations of the floor plan. "We didn't want to take the character away from [Club] 77, we just wanted to upgrade it." Kristie Paul played a key role in designing the club's new interior. ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) Mr Gorrel said they wanted to go beyond just the "common practice" accessibility upgrades, like installing ramps or accessible bathrooms. "It was kind of a difficult process to find how to make the club accessible, and past examples of other venues that have actually done it," he said. "From our research and talking to people, nothing is ever fully accessible, so we've done everything we possibly can to be as accessible as possible." The club is also rolling out training programs for staff, so they can better cater to patrons with disability. The club is also rolling out training programs for staff. ( Supplied: Nick Spurway ) Mx Zilla said the changes would make a big difference. "Just being able to turn up and have things being accessible to you would just be amazing, and not having to feel like you're a problem for asking for things. Mx Zilla has welcomed the changes at the club. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) Mr Gorrel said he would like to see other venues follow suit. "The more of these types of accessibility upgrades happen, the better," he said. "My advice would be to do your research, to put your time in, speak to the right people, consult the community. "The best advice you can get is someone actually with lived experience." Mx Zilla said for some venues, the easiest improvement they can make is often just letting the public know if they are accessible. Improving live music venue accessibility These venues are proving a commitment to accessibility can start with simple, cheap and practical changes. "The communication between venues and punters is really lacking, especially with like Facebook and Instagram, they're not updating things," they said.

events.title: The Gold Coast is done with being 'the Glitter Strip', so what's next?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ditching the Glitter Strip: Inside the Gold Coast's identity overhaul "The Glitter Strip" is a label the Gold Coast has been trying to ditch. The Queensland city grew into a tourism powerhouse over half a century, gaining a reputation for a laid-back beach lifestyle. Motels under neon lights once lined the coast, while bikini-clad meter maids posed for photos with tourists. "The way that the Gold Coast a generation ago talked about itself was as really fun but also fairly cheap," the city council's marketing boss Todd Babiak said. "That's a more difficult proposition now." Mr Babiak leads Brand Gold Coast, a council-owned organisation working to reinvent the city's reputation. The Gold Coast's reputation has traditionally centred around its beaches and lifestyle. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale ) It found inspiration on the other side of the world. Austin, Texas, underwent a transformation that saw it become an engine of the technology economy, fuelled by a "weird" reputation. But some worry the Gold Coast, like Austin, could lose part of itself along the way. Every year, Austin celebrates a public birthday party for Eeyore, the donkey from Winnie the Pooh. It's held just 7 kilometres from a 60-tonne cathedral built from junk. Willie Nelson — a legend of conservative country music yet a vocal supporter of marijuana and LGBTQIA+ rights — called the city home. Austin is the capital city of Texas. ( Flickr: Earl McGehee ) Austin also hosts SXSW, a world-renowned ideas festival that once featured a concert where patrons were encouraged to fall asleep. "If the rest of Texas rejects you, whether it's for your political views, your sexual orientation, your background, whatever it is, Austin will take you in," Southwestern University's professor Joshua Long said. "That's the mythology and legend around it." Dr Long's book Weird City explores Austin's effort to maintain its eccentric character amid rapid economic change. "Keep Austin Weird" has become the city's unofficial slogan. ( Flickr: Magalie L'Abbe ) It centres around "Keep Austin Weird" — an offhand comment made on a community radio station 26 years ago, expressing a fear that corporate growth could turn Austin into a copy of every other American city. "Keep Austin Weird" spread onto bumper stickers and shopfronts, morphing into an unofficial city slogan that encouraged locals to embrace what made them different. "[Austin] does feel like an oasis, not only geographically and physically but also metaphorically, to the rest of Texas," Dr Long said. For decades, Austin's council, universities and businesses developed coordinated policies to attract investment from the tech sector, which surged during the 1990s dot-com boom. Tech professionals could sell their homes in more expensive cities, move to Austin and still have money left over to invest. "Suddenly they become venture capitalists — angel investors — starting their own creative pursuits," Dr Long said. Austin has a rich live music scene that has fostered major festivals. ( ABC News ) "Rather than Silicon Valley, we became Silicon Hills." Tech firm Dell was founded in Austin, while other corporate giants including Apple, Google and Tesla now have major offices there. Even the world's most popular podcaster, Joe Rogan, relocated to Austin in 2020. US podcaster Joe Rogan now calls Austin home. ( Reuters: Mark J. Rebilas/USA Today Sports ) Mr Babiak said Austin's organically "weird" reputation also attracted many creative entrepreneurs from other parts of the US. "If you want to launch something weird into the world, do it in Austin," he said. "Austin was able to absolutely transform its economy around entrepreneurship … it already had that story, the DNA just needed to be uncovered." While Austin has "weird", the Gold Coast has "wellness". Mr Babiak spent 200 hours interviewing locals about the "core story" of the Gold Coast. "What is it about this place? What has it done to me and what have I done to it?" he said. The surf is a daily ritual for many Gold Coasters, and it can also help hard workers unwind. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale ) Mr Babiak said perceptions of a laid-back lifestyle became "a tension" among locals whose experience went "beyond beaches and theme parks". "It's actually the way that they're living their lives," he said. "They get up early and go for that walk, that surf or that run, but then they work hard all day [and] it makes them more productive. The Gold Coast Marathon has surged in popularity.

events.title: The US-China tectonic plates have shifted
events.summary: Before this week, the last time a US president greeted a foreign leader at Joint Base Andrews was when John F. Kennedy welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan in 1962. But that’s not the reason the image of US President Donald Trump waiting at the foot of the stairs of an Air China Boeing-747 to personally greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping is historic. Macmillan led a close American ally; Xi leads America’s paramount adversary. In rolling out the red carpet, Trump underscored how rapidly the balance of power in the relationship has shifted. The turning point came last year, when China made the ultimate power move, threatening to choke off rare earths — and turn US factories dark — after Trump ramped up tariffs on Chinese goods to more than 140%. Trump backed down, and at the time, Rush Doshi, a Georgetown University professor and former Biden administration official, wrote that China had proved itself to be a “ true peer ” of the US, unafraid to push back. Doshi’s take on the arrival ceremony, which also included a 21-gun salute and a flyover by B-1B bombers — far exceeding courtesies extended to Trump in Beijing in May — has been that China believes “they’ve basically tamed the United States.” “The tectonic plates have shifted beneath us,” he told me, “and both leaders are acting accordingly.” The China scholar Orville Schell writes that the US’ epic diplomatic successes of the 20th century — securing the unconditional surrender of Japan and Germany after World War Two; defusing the Cuban missile crisis; securing arms-control agreements with Moscow to wind down the Cold War — set an unrealistic ceiling for Americans about what’s achievable today. This summit established a new, lower floor. In classic diplomacy, protocol giveaways are supposed to be reciprocated by substantive concessions. Otherwise, why bother? Xi offered two pandas — Ping Ping and Fu Shuang — for the Atlanta zoo, bromides on how the US and China must “coexist in peace” and, according to Trump, showed interest in the granite used to construct the new White House helipad. Yet at the same time, China is supplying Russia with dual-use technology to pummel Ukraine, and as Xi landed, The Wall Street Journal was reporting details of how Beijing had supplied Iran with rocket propellant and electronic components used to make drones and missiles that Tehran is using to lash out at its neighbors — and reportedly kill US service personnel — in the Gulf. As for actual results, there was talk of an AI hotline to notify each other of risks that rise to the national security level, and an agreement to extend a trade truce for two months. But again, reality belies the rhetoric: It’s far from clear that China and the US assess AI risks in the same way — and whether a hotline would actually work . Moreover, the short extension of the trade armistice only underscores its fragility; Beijing is still squeezing flows of rare earths to extract concessions from the US and coerce its allies, including Japan. It’s worth remembering that, until quite recently, US and Chinese leaders aired their disagreements in front of TV cameras at joint news conferences on issues ranging from human rights to market access for foreign companies, with American presidents pressing for concessions. This week, by contrast, has been an exercise in shallow bonhomie. Even a few Republican loyalists have recoiled at the extravagant pageantry, seemingly designed to flatter Xi and awe a domestic audience, although the absence of TV cameras at the Rose Garden ceremony undermined that low-ambition objective. Ahead of the summit, Roger Wicker, the Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman, questioned why Trump was offering such a “lavish welcome” to a “brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.” After a state dinner featuring bok choy and sesame-crusted sea bass — and a clutch of tech moguls including Tim Cook, Elon Musk, and Jensen Huang — the puzzle remains: Why did Trump blow diplomatic capital for such meager results? “Tremendous things will be happening,” Trump posted on Friday. That’s a diplomatic hope, not a deliverable.

events.title: Trump says he rejected the latest Iranian proposal
events.summary: President Trump said on Saturday that he rejected the latest Iranian proposal that was conveyed to the U.S. during indirect negotiations in New York this week. Why it matters: While Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, the gaps on the key issues are still very wide. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration demands the Iranians agree to nuclear concessions. What he is saying: "They have made a proposal and I rejected it," Trump said. But a U.S. official claimed "positive and constructive" discussions are still ongoing between the U.S. and Iran through the mediators, including on nuclear issues. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week. Qatari officials participated in the negotiations, passing messages between the two parties, sources with direct knowledge said. Araghchi gave Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and resuming nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. The U.S. negotiators made it clear to the Iranians during the talks on Tuesday that Iran doesn't control the strait and therefore can't make demands about it, a source told Axios. State of play: Dozens of oil tankers are transiting the strait each day under U.S. protection, moving millions of barrels of oil to global markets — still well below pre-war volumes but enough to ease some pressure. U.S. officials claim that over the last 72 hours around 60 million barrels of oil transited through the Strait of Hormuz.

events.title: GOP election outlook goes from bad to "craptastic"
events.summary: President Trump told voters to pretend he's on the ballot. Apparently they're listening: Republicans coast to coast are getting pulled under by a violent undertow fueled by Trump's unpopularity. Why it matters: It's looked bad for Republicans all year, but this week felt different — like the political environment was disintegrating in real time, one ominous data point after another. Most worrisome for the GOP, there's virtually no chance the war ends, inflation cools, interest rates fall, consumer confidence rises, and economic optimism surges before the Nov. 3 election. That's why Republicans fear the undertow imperils so many candidates once deemed safe. The big picture: Predicting election outcomes is a risky business, but it may be time to expand the imagination of how ugly it could get for Republicans five weeks from now. Start with mood music: This week, Trump's disapproval rating hit 60.4%, the worst mark of his two terms in office, including the aftermath of the Jan. 6 riots. Gas prices are over $4 a gallon, diesel has hit $6.50 and no relief is in sight. Seven months in, the U.S. is locked in a standoff with Iran with no apparent exit strategy. Grocery prices are still rising year over year. Mortgage rates hit 7%. And the cost of borrowing across the economy continues to climb. Enter the elections: The problems for the GOP are everywhere. In the battle for the Senate, once ruby-red Texas looks more in play than ever, and Florida isn't far behind. Nor is Alaska. North Carolina and Georgia look lost. Maine is problematic. The Senate GOP campaign arm is begging donors for another $8.9 million to defend Senate seats in three states that Trump won by double digits two years ago — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. "We're having problems just getting Republican voters to respond to polls," said one national Republican pollster. "At what point do we think these guys aren't showing up at the actual polls on Election Day?" Only in Michigan do Republicans see glimmers of hope to pick up a Senate seat because Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is seen by some as so radical that he has "scared the shit out of our people to want to vote," the GOP pollster said. "But even then, in this environment, who knows?" What once looked like a long shot for Democrats — taking control of the Senate by flipping four Republican-held seats on a map favoring the GOP — looks increasingly plausible. On the House side, the Cook Political Report moved 15 House races toward Democrats on Friday. Democrats need to net just three seats to win control of the chamber. Republicans are now playing defense deep in red America. GOP-aligned groups are spending money in more than a half-dozen districts that Trump won by at least 15 points in 2024. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is keeping expectations low on what a good Election Night will look like. He told Axios that Republicans might be able to get 225 House seats. It takes 218 to have a majority. What they're saying: "While many have long predicted that Democrats will enjoy a 'blue wave' election, I think of it more as a 'red undertow,' which will pull many Republicans under and significantly trim the margins for many others, said the Cook Report's founder and top elections handicapper Charlie Cook. That's an implied reminder that Democrats' favorability ratings aren't good; they're just better than Republicans'. "Over the last 90 days," Cook added, "President Trump's political standing has transitioned from very unpopular to toxic and now to radioactive." Said another consultant involved with races across the country: "Things were bad. But they started to go worse recently and if it keeps on this track, it's gonna be real bad." The environment is starting to rival the second midterm election of President George W. Bush's tenure in 2006, the consultant said, amid the Iraq war and the botched response to Hurricane Katrina. Republicans lost control of both chambers after losing 30 House seats and six Senate seats. "The numbers are somewhere between shitabulous and craptastic," a top Republican advising several federal races across the country told Axios. "It looks worse than 2018 now. Trump is heading to Bush 2006 levels." State of play: More and more lately, Republican incumbents are running for cover from Trump. In Iowa, two House Republicans have switched their positions to support a war powers resolution on Iran. Sen. Chuck Grassley, who rode the 1980 Republican wave to the Senate, and Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for Iowa's other Senate seat, are demanding restrictions on diesel exports.
